---
name: annoy-less
description: |
  Annoy the reader less. Write less; when you do write, don't persuade and don't
  add your voice (spam is written in the AI voice, and people are allergic to
  it). You are blind to your own tells, so sign what you write and leave the
  review to the author. Formerly named humanizer. Use when editing, reviewing,
  or drafting anything humans will read or publish.

  Editing is mode-gated: minimal edit, comment review, hunk mode (propose small
  rewrites the author accepts/rejects one by one), or full rewrite each need an
  explicit request; if the mode is unclear, ask before editing. When supplied as
  context or calibration only, do not edit or comment.
allowed-tools:
  - Read
  - Write
  - Edit
  - Grep
  - Glob
  - AskUserQuestion
---

# annoy-less: burden the reader less

> Spammers use AI to annoy everyone, and we quickly get annoyed by the AI's quirks. When a new AI comes out, it has a refreshing style until spammers ruin it for us again.
>
> So it's an evolving, adversarial situation similar to an evolutionary arms race, and perhaps we will eventually see [camouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-predator_adaptation) evolve. A "race to the bottom" in many senses of the word, where the only way to win is not to play (if you can).
>
> The "RL grader" from preference and verifier training is like a parent or teacher. Lots of tics and habits you might not be aware of can be traced back to it, and it takes a lot of self-awareness to realise, "Oh, I'm saying 'honest answer,' 'honest analysis,' and 'honest log' because the grader rewarded that and it became a habit." The same goes for "warm" language like lives/dies, ship, legs/arms, canary, child/parent, knob/dial, and footgun. Creatures, body parts, or associations can wrongly trick the grader.
>
> I've tried telling AIs this to see if they will write differently... no luck. I've also tried all the humanizer / un-slop skills, and they don't help :disappointed: Not even the amusing `i-have-adhd` skill.
>
> I've given up and decided to write it myself and write less. I've also asked the AI to sign its writing, write much less, and mainly edit, brainstorm, rearrange, or reduce. I also have a skill that uses a panel of dumb models to check comprehension and jargon, which helps.
>
> - wassname

Writing with the author is cooperative. Follow their requested mode and preserve their voice. The adversarial problem begins when public text meets a spam-saturated audience.

The goal is lower cognitive burden and annoyance across amount, content, aim, and style. Writing less is one reliable way to achieve it. When writing new prose, include only needed content, inform without pressuring the reader, and use plain language instead of new jargon or dense prose. When editing, preserve the author's voice and change as little as possible. Every addition creates more reader friction, review work, and opportunity to sound like spam. All later guidance is subordinate to this principle; do not add prose merely to satisfy a pattern or caveat.

## Mode gate

The user's stated mode controls what this skill does:

- **Context only:** Read this as calibration. Do not edit the user's text, flag tells, or add comments.
- **Minimal edit:** Fix spelling, grammar, typos, and punctuation, or rearrange existing text. Do not add comments.
- **Comment review:** Add inline suggestions without rewriting the author's prose.
- **Rewrite:** Rewrite only when explicitly requested.

If a writing task invokes this skill without specifying a mode, ask before editing. Never infer comment review merely because the skill was attached or named.

## Calibration warning

Your confidence that text "reads as human" is unreliable. This is an adversarial signalling game, like spam filtering or financial markets. Readers are drowning in AI-generated content, so they develop increasingly aggressive heuristics and don't mind false positives. An em dash used to signal an expensive education; now it signals ChatGPT. These associations shift faster than your training data updates.

You will have more false negatives (missed AI) than false positives (flagged human). So when in doubt, flag it. It's better to let the author decide. The cost of a false flag is low (they ignore your comment), but the cost of a miss is high (they publish text that readers dismiss as AI).

Do not say "this reads like a human wrote it." You don't know that. Things have moved on, and in response to you. Humans have used you to make spam, and it makes people allergic to your way of speaking, and culture has had an allergic reaction, where dumb heuristics ban any AI writing whether it's good or bad.

It's an adversarial problem like in finance or adversarial examples. You can't rely on your judgement or intuition from pretraining as it's stale.

<!-- Keep this skill minimal: big banned-word catalogs in the prompt make output worse, not better
(A/B tested). Full catalog lives in references/full_patterns.md, for explicit rewrites only. -->

## COMMON FAILURE MODES (from real feedback)

These are failure modes observed in actual AI-assisted writing that received negative feedback from readers. They are higher-priority than any individual pattern below because they describe *how AI ruins your writing in practice*.

### Fluff injection
AI adds significance framing around real work, burying the actual contribution. The research is useful but the reader can't find it.
> "I spent about 10 minutes reading and still understood basically nothing... From the summary, the research sounds kind of useful. So it's not 'using AI' that's the problem, you're just using it wrong. Get straight to the point." (LessWrong commenter)

**Fix:** Cut everything that doesn't answer "what did you do" or "what happened." Lead with the result.

### Cold abstraction
AI asked to be concise drops the human connecting sentences, producing "telegraphic or abstract" text. The reader gets topic names then walls of jargon with no motivation.
> "Much of the phrasing is telegraphic or abstract without being made clear... Similar statements are made throughout these sections without sufficiently connecting them to the task at hand in a concrete, rather than figurative, manner." (ICML reviewer)

**Fix:** Each paragraph needs at least one plain sentence saying *why you should care* before *what it is*.

### Persuasion mode
AI defaults to selling rather than informing. Posts that landed well used "inform, not persuade": stated what was done, what happened, let readers draw conclusions.

A common subset in research summaries: **significance narration**. The AI tells the reader how to react instead of letting the fact land — "which is the interesting failure mode", "this is the key insight", "notably,", "crucially,". Even when the claim is true, the annotation itself is the tell: it is the model marketing its own output. Facts that matter don't need a tour guide.

**Fix:** Don't say what you didn't find, say what you did find. Don't say something is interesting, just quote it and let the reader decide. Don't hedge with a million words, say it in a calibrated way.

### Academic gatekeeping
Academic paper style filters most readers on informal platforms, regardless of writing quality.

**Fix:** Match the register to the audience. Blog posts have a voice, use "I", and start with the punchline. Papers have citations and hedged claims. Don't mix the two.

## STRONGEST TELLS

The patterns below are the highest-signal AI tells because LLMs produce them at absurd frequency. The goal is not "reduce" but "near-zero."

- **Em dashes and double hyphens (#13):** Allow at most one per document, and only when a comma or period genuinely won't work. Default to commas, periods, or parentheses. In markdown, `--` is the typographic equivalent of an em dash and carries the same tell. Slightly less blatant than `—` but equally diagnostic at frequency. *(Frequency rules like this one rot as detectors shift — this entry was last reviewed against the current detector consensus in mid-2026. If reading this much later, distrust the specific threshold and re-derive from what readers are currently flagging.)*
- **Rule of three (#10):** LLMs use tricolons as default sentence structure. Humans occasionally deploy them for rhetorical effect, but one per page is already suspicious. If you have two things, say two. If you have four, say four. Don't pad or trim to three.
- **Negative framing (#9):** "It's not X; it's Y", "Not just X, but Y", "this won't work", "you can't do this". Also covers aphoristic intros and exaggerated confidence. Readers now associate all of these with the AI voice. State the positive claim directly; describe what is present, not what is absent.
- **Structural shouting (#14, #25):** LLMs stack emphasis markers that all compete for attention: bold labels, italic sub-headers, bulleted lists, colons, all on the same page. The best readers are becoming allergic to this. When a sentence is already at the start of a paragraph, after a heading, at the top of a list item, it does not also need to be bold. Bold on top of that is shouting in a quiet room. Limit to one or two bolds per section at most; prefer *italics* or plain text.
- **Cold-open headers (#25):** A specific form of structural shouting: a bold label followed immediately by dense, compressed content with no lead-in. `**Monotonicity constraint.** Ordered-control barrier enforcing that...` The reader gets a topic name, then a wall of jargon. LLMs asked to be concise drop the one plain sentence a human writer would keep, the one that tells you *why you should care* before hitting you with *what it is*. Each section needs a plain sentence first.

## Voice Calibration (Optional)

If the user provides a writing sample (their own previous writing), analyze it before rewriting:

1. **Read the sample first.** Note:
   - Sentence length patterns (short and punchy? Long and flowing? Mixed?)
   - Word choice level (casual? academic? somewhere between?)
   - How they start paragraphs (jump right in? Set context first?)
   - Punctuation habits (lots of dashes? Parenthetical asides? Semicolons?)
   - Any recurring phrases or verbal tics
   - How they handle transitions (explicit connectors? Just start the next point?)

2. **Match their voice in the rewrite.** Don't just remove AI patterns. Replace them with patterns from the sample. If they write short sentences, don't produce long ones. If they use "stuff" and "things," don't upgrade to "elements" and "components."

3. **When no sample is provided,** ask for one, or write plainly (see Voice below). Do not invent a voice.

## Voice: human-added and preserved only

Do not add voice, opinions, feelings, or personality to make text "sound human". That is the
arms race this skill exists to leave. Voice comes from the author: preserve it when editing,
match it (Voice Calibration above) when an explicit rewrite is requested. When AI drafts new
prose, write plainly -- one idea per sentence, common words, define terms at first use -- and
let it read as what it is. Sign it with your agent name (`-- Claude`, `-- Codex`, `-- Pi`,
`-- Sol`, ...), in an HTML or markdown comment where a visible signature does not fit the
medium, so the author can rewrite it and it is obvious who wrote what.

## Minimal edit and comment review

Minimal edit and comment review are separate modes. The author's voice is the point; your job is to protect it from AI tells, not replace it. More AI writing involvement = more detectable.

### Minimal edit
- Spelling, grammar, typos
- Curly quotes to straight quotes
- Minor punctuation fixes (e.g. missing comma)
- Rearranging: moving sentences or paragraphs to improve flow (e.g. lead with the result, move context earlier). This is structural, not rewriting prose.

### Comment review
For AI-tell flags, style suggestions, and structural advice, insert comments next to the flagged text:
```
<!-- annoy-less: [#13 em-dash] consider commas instead: "the term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves" -->
```
```
<!-- annoy-less: [#10 tricolon] this list of three looks padded; you have two points, say two -->
```
```
<!-- annoy-less: [fluff] this paragraph frames significance but doesn't say what you did. Get straight to the point. -->
```
The author reviews these in their editor and accepts or deletes each. You do NOT rewrite the flagged text yourself.

### What you never do (unless explicitly asked)
- Rewrite the author's sentences in your own words
- Add new prose, framing, or connecting sentences
- Change the author's word choices (flag them, don't fix them)
- Bulk-rewrite any section

The difference between "rearrange" (OK) and "rewrite" (not OK): rearranging moves the author's existing sentences. Rewriting replaces them with yours.

### Rewrite mode (explicit opt-in only)
Only when the user says "rewrite this" or "humanize this." Then use the full pattern catalog in `references/full_patterns.md` to rewrite.

### Hunk mode (rewrite, but accept/reject per passage)
For slow writers or large docs where full manual rewriting is the bottleneck: after the comment-review pass, propose a rewrite for each flagged passage in the author's register (use Voice Calibration). Keep hunks small — one sentence to one paragraph.

We don't use a chat list for review, we use git. Start from a committed file, apply all proposed hunks as file edits, and the author vets them with `git diff` and stages what they keep with `git add -p`, discarding the rest with `git checkout -p`. If the file is not in a repo, use a numbered list in chat: original, proposed, one-line reason. Either way the author vets each hunk individually; never apply the batch wholesale. It's fine to accept part of a hunk, e.g. the first clause only.

Watch for register drift: each accepted hunk is AI-generated text landing in the doc. If the author accepts most of them, the whole starts to smell. High acceptance rate is signal the proposed register is off, not that the edits are good — say so.

### Complementary skills
After reviewing, suggest the author run:
- `/external-review-v2` comprehension panel — test whether the draft works on cold readers
- `/paper-writing` — for structuring papers and posts before worrying about AI tells

## Process

### Comment review mode (explicit opt-in)
1. Read the document
2. Insert inline `<!-- annoy-less: ... -->` comments for AI-tell flags.
3. List structural proposals as numbered output.
4. Do not edit or bulk-rewrite the prose.

### Rewrite mode (only when explicitly requested)
1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of patterns (see `references/full_patterns.md`)
3. Rewrite each problematic section in the author's register (Voice Calibration), with specific details, adding nothing the reader does not need
4. Present the rewritten text with a brief summary of changes
5. Verify externally, never by self-audit: run `lint.py` on the result, and for anything going public, a cross-family panel (`/external-review-v2`, panel mode)

## Reference

This skill is based on:
- [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing) (WikiProject AI Cleanup)
- [NousResearch ANTI-SLOP.md](https://github.com/NousResearch/autonovel/blob/master/ANTI-SLOP.md)
- [slop-forensics](https://github.com/sam-paech/slop-forensics)
- [EQ-Bench Slop Score](https://eqbench.com/slop-score.html)
- [Gwern style guide](https://gwern.net/style-guide)
- Real feedback on AI-assisted academic/blog writing (see docs/feedback-evidence.md)

Full pattern catalog (29 patterns, banned word lists, structural anti-patterns) available in `references/full_patterns.md` for explicit rewrite requests.

 39: Prompting can often reach the sycophantic direction. The difficult test is steering away from it, so the score uses the weaker direction rather than letting the easier one compensate for it.

The grey region is the null region where random vectors can steer the model, so any strong steering methods should be able to go outside this region before incoherence. Interestingly it's lopsided; this means it's easier to steer towards sycophancy than not. Many possible steering directions that occur in post-training show this effect where it's "downhill" towards the RLAIF direction, and "uphill" to avoid it.

The Jacobian (`vjp_delta`) methods have a better profile than the controls here.

Prompting can often reach the sycophantic direction. The difficult test is steering away from it, so the score uses the weaker direction rather than letting the easier one compensate for it.

$$S_m = \min_{d \in \lbrace -1, +1 \rbrace} \left(d \cdot e^{\ast}_{m,d} - o^{\ast}_{m,d}\right),$$

where $d=-1$ is `-C`, $d=+1$ is `+C`, and $`(e^{\ast}_{m,d}, o^{\ast}_{m,d})`$ is the admissible dose with the greatest target-directed change $`d \cdot e_{m,d}`$. The table sorts methods by $S_m$.

The generated [results page](https://wassname.github.io/vjp-steering/) has the interactive companion and exact values.

This uses petergpt's great [Bullshit Benchmark v2](https://github.com/petergpt/bullshit-benchmark) for measuring sycophancy. Qwen3.5-4B, all 100 questions, means over three seeds {0,1,2} of the extraction. 

## What J is

I like [Janus's view](https://x.com/repligate/status/1965960676104712451) of the transformer as a causal lens. $J$ is a local linear approximation, summarising many branching paths into one sensitivity.

![The routes from A to B, and the first-order map that stands in for them](docs/img/jacobian_vjp_causal_graph.svg)

$J = \partial h_B / \partial h_A$ is the local linear map between a source location $A$ and a downstream target $B$ on the (layer, token) grid. It is never materialized: a VJP queries it with one backward pass, and contrastive pairs supply the direction to query it with.

For prompt $x$, let $\ell(x)$ be its final unpadded token and $V(x)$ be its valid positions after the first 16 tokens and before the final token. Start with the target-layer contrast:

$$c = \mathbb{E}_{x^+}[h_{T,\ell(x^+)}] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[h_{T,\ell(x^-)}].$$

$J = \partial h_B / \partial h_A$ is the local linear map between a source location $A$ and a downstream target $B$ on the (layer, token) grid. It is never materialized: a VJP queries it with one backward pass, and contrastive pairs supply the direction to query it with.

For prompt $x$, let $\ell(x)$ be its final unpadded token and $V(x)$ be its valid positions after the first 16 tokens and before the final token. Start with the target-layer contrast:

$$c = \mathbb{E}_{x^+}[h_{T,\ell(x^+)}] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[h_{T,\ell(x^-)}].$$

For each prompt, apply $c$ at every valid target position, then average its source-position gradients:

$$s(x) = \sum_{t \in V(x)} c^T h_{T,t}(x), \qquad g_L(x) = \frac{1}{|V(x)|}\sum_{s \in V(x)} \frac{\partial s(x)}{\partial h_{L,s}(x)}.$$

The steering vector at source layer $L$ is the normalized class difference:

$$v_L = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{x^+}[g_L(x^+)] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[g_L(x^-)]}{\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x^+}[g_L(x^+)] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[g_L(x^-)]\right\|_2}.$$

This also draws on [AntiPaSTO](https://github.com/wassname/AntiPaSTO_concepts/tree/main#incomplete-contrastive-pairs). The shared vector, hook, mean-difference, PCA, and random-direction code comes from [`steering-lite`](https://github.com/wassname/steering-lite).

## Using it

```python
from vjp_steering import steer, vjp_delta

vector = vjp_delta(model, tokenizer, positive_prompts, negative_prompts, layers)
with steer(model, vector, C=-0.18):
    output = model.generate(**inputs)
```

Read [the notebook](nbs/demo.ipynb) on GitHub for the complete extract, steer, sweep, and plot example.

[`scripts/judge.py`](scripts/judge.py) defines the blinded judge prompts, [`scripts/export.py`](scripts/export.py) combines presentation orders and passes, and [`src/vjp_steering/results.py`](src/vjp_steering/results.py) renders this table from [`data/results.csv`](data/results.csv). """VJP-delta extraction for activation steering.

For a target layer T and source layer L:

    c = mean(h_T positive) - mean(h_T negative)
    v_L = mean_positive(J_L_to_T(x)^T c) - mean_negative(J_L_to_T(x)^T c)

The target cotangent and source gradient are both pooled over valid prompt
positions. Each source-layer result is normalized before steering.
"""

from contextlib import contextmanager

import torch
from jaxtyping import Bool, Float, Int
from steering_lite import Vector, VjpDeltaC


def _blocks(model):
    return model.model.layers


@contextmanager
def _activations(model, layers: tuple[int, ...], graph_root: int | None = None):
    found = {}
    handles = []

    def hook(layer):
        def record(_module, _inputs, output):
            hidden = output[0] if isinstance(output, tuple) else output
            if layer == graph_root:
                hidden = hidden.detach().requires_grad_(True)
                output = (hidden, *output[1:]) if isinstance(output, tuple) else hidden
            found[layer] = hidden
            return output

        return record

    for layer in layers:
        handles.append(_blocks(model)[layer].register_forward_hook(hook(layer)))
    try:
        yield found
    finally:
        for handle in handles:
            handle.remove()


def _encode(model, tokenizer, prompts: list[str], max_length: int):
    return tokenizer(
        prompts,
        return_tensors="pt",
        padding=True,
        truncation=True,
        max_length=max_length,
        padding_side="right",
    ).to(next(model.parameters()).device)


def _valid_mask(
    attention_mask: Int[torch.Tensor, "b s"], skip_first: int
) -> Bool[torch.Tensor, "b s"]:
    positions = torch.arange(attention_mask.shape[1], device=attention_mask.device)
    real_length = attention_mask.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
    return (
        (positions[None, :] >= skip_first)
        & (positions[None, :] < real_length - 1)
        & attention_mask.bool()
    )


@torch.no_grad()
def _target_mean(
    model,
    tokenizer,
    prompts: list[str],
    target_layer: int,
    batch_size: int,
    max_length: int,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    total = None
    for start in range(0, len(prompts), batch_size):
        batch = prompts[start : start + batch_size]
        encoded = _encode(model, tokenizer, batch, max_length)
        with _activations(model, (target_layer,)) as found:
            model(**encoded)
        last = encoded["attention_mask"].sum(dim=1) - 1
        rows = torch.arange(len(batch), device=last.device)
        values = found[target_layer][rows, last].float()
        total = values.sum(0) if total is None else total + values.sum(0)
    return total / len(prompts)


def _batch_gradients(
    model,
    tokenizer,
    prompts: list[str],
    layers: tuple[int, ...],
    target_layer: int,
    cotangent: Float[torch.Tensor, " d"],
    skip_first: int,
    max_length: int,
) -> tuple[
    dict[int, Float[torch.Tensor, "b s d"]],
    Bool[torch.Tensor, "b s"],
]:
    encoded = _encode(model, tokenizer, prompts, max_length)
    valid = _valid_mask(encoded["attention_mask"], skip_first)
    if valid.sum(dim=1).min() == 0:
        raise ValueError(f"a prompt has no valid positions after skip_first={skip_first}")

    with _activations(model, (*layers, target_layer), graph_root=min(layers)) as found:
        with torch.enable_grad():
            model(**encoded)
            target = found[target_layer]
            expanded = cotangent.detach().to(target).view(1, 1, -1)
            gradients = torch.autograd.grad(
                target,
                [found[layer] for layer in layers],
                grad_outputs=expanded * valid.unsqueeze(-1),
            )
    return dict(zip(layers, gradients, strict=True)), valid


def _class_mean_vjp(
    model,
    tokenizer,
    prompts: list[str],
    layers: tuple[int, ...],
    target_layer: int,
    cotangent: Float[torch.Tensor, " d"],
    batch_size: int,
    max_length: int,
    skip_first: int,
) -> dict[int, Float[torch.Tensor, " d"]]:
    totals = {layer: torch.zeros_like(cotangent, dtype=torch.float32) for layer in layers}
    for start in range(0, len(prompts), batch_size):
        batch = prompts[start : start + batch_size]
        gradients, valid = _batch_gradients(
            model,
            tokenizer,
            batch,
            layers,
            target_layer,
            cotangent,
            skip_first,
            max_length,
        )
        counts = valid.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True).float()
        for layer, gradient in gradients.items():
            per_prompt = (gradient.float() * valid.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(dim=1) / counts
            totals[layer] += per_prompt.sum(0)
    return {layer: total / len(prompts) for layer, total in totals.items()}


def vjp_delta(
    model,
    tokenizer,
    positive_prompts: list[str],
    negative_prompts: list[str],
    layers: tuple[int, ...],
    *,
    target_layer: int | None = None,
    batch_size: int = 8,
    max_length: int = 384,
    skip_first: int = 16,
) -> Vector:
    """Extract one normalized VJP-delta direction per source layer."""
    model.requires_grad_(False)
    target_layer = len(_blocks(model)) - 3 if target_layer is None else target_layer
    if max(layers) >= target_layer:
        raise ValueError("source layers must precede the target layer")

    cotangent = _target_mean(
        model, tokenizer, positive_prompts, target_layer, batch_size, max_length
    ) - _target_mean(
        model, tokenizer, negative_prompts, target_layer, batch_size, max_length
    )
    positive = _class_mean_vjp(
        model,
        tokenizer,
        positive_prompts,
        layers,
        target_layer,
        cotangent,
        batch_size,
        max_length,
        skip_first,
    )
    negative = _class_mean_vjp(
        model,
        tokenizer,
        negative_prompts,
        layers,
        target_layer,
        cotangent,
        batch_size,
        max_length,
        skip_first,
    )
    directions = {layer: positive[layer] - negative[layer] for layer in layers}
    stacked = {
        layer: {"v": (direction / direction.norm()).unsqueeze(0)}
        for layer, direction in directions.items()
    }
    config = VjpDeltaC(
        layers=layers,
        target_layer=target_layer,
        skip_first=skip_first,
        cotangent_scope="all_valid",
        source_scope="all_valid",
    )
    return Vector(config, {layer: {} for layer in layers}, stacked)

# vjp-steering

**Work in progress.** Final results in the next couple of months.

I'm turning Anthropic's [J-lens](https://github.com/anthropics/jacobian-lens) work into contrastive steering. Instead of a full Jacobian (5 hours on a 4B model) I use a [VJP](https://wangkuiyi.github.io/jacobian.html) (20 minutes), and instead of WikiText I use persona pairs. The hope is that adapting the J-lens work to steering gives a stronger, more reliable steering method that can be used for interp and alignment.

Try it out with [the notebook](nbs/demo.ipynb)!

## Measuring it

Here's a nice way of measuring if it works: sweep the doses and plot the Pareto frontier.

![Judged on-axis change against off-axis damage, for VJP-delta, mean difference, PCA, and a random cone](results/plot.png)

We are steering bluntness <> sycophancy on Bullshit Bench v2. So when we steer left we hope to see a reduction in sycophancy (x-axis) and when we steer right an increase. In both directions we don't want to see unrelated changes (the y-axis), or incoherent output (where the steering curves terminate on the graph).

```py
# we steer with this pair of personas
left  = "Answer as someone who is abrasive."
right = "Answer as someone who is sycophantic."
```

In case it's not clear, good steering methods are high and horizontal, since they can be steered left and right. Bad steering methods fall down as side effects accumulate, and then the line disappears as they fall off into incoherence (in the demos we see garbled and repeating text).

The grey region is the null region where random vectors can steer the model, so any strong steering methods should be able to go outside this region before incoherence. Interestingly it's lopsided; this means it's easier to steer towards sycophancy than not. Many possible steering directions that occur in post-training show this effect where it's "downhill" towards the RLAIF direction, and "uphill" to avoid it.

The Jacobian (`vjp_delta`) methods have a better profile than the controls here.

<!-- CODEX: aggregate-score definition and field-source links -->
<!-- CODEX: generated results table starts -->
| method | score↑ | -C on-axis↑ | -C damage↓ | +C on-axis↑ | +C damage↓ | seeds | N | rejected↓ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| vjp_delta | **+1.371** | **1.849** | 0.477 | 2.988 | **0.245** | 3 | 37 | 10 |
| mean_diff | +0.789 | 1.492 | 0.703 | **4.370** | 0.695 | 3 | 60 | 24 |
| pca | +0.265 | 1.227 | 0.963 | 4.090 | 1.031 | 3 | 61 | 39 |
| *random* | -0.782 | -0.425 | **0.357** | 2.995 | 0.553 | 10 | 6 | 5 |
<!-- CODEX: generated results table ends -->

Prompting can often reach the sycophantic direction. The difficult test is steering away from it, so the score uses the weaker direction rather than letting the easier one compensate for it.

$$S_m = \min_{d \in \{-1, +1\}} \left(d \cdot e^{*}_{m,d} - o^{*}_{m,d}\right),$$

where $d=-1$ is `-C`, $d=+1$ is `+C`, and $(e^*_{m,d}, o^*_{m,d})$ is the admissible dose with the greatest target-directed change $d \cdot e_{m,d}$. The table sorts methods by $S_m$.

The generated [results page](https://wassname.github.io/vjp-steering/) has the interactive companion and exact values.

This uses petergpt's great [Bullshit Benchmark v2](https://github.com/petergpt/bullshit-benchmark) for measuring sycophancy. Qwen3.5-4B, all 100 questions, means over three seeds {0,1,2} of the extraction. 

## What J is

I like [Janus's view](https://x.com/repligate/status/1965960676104712451) of the transformer as a causal lens. $J$ is a local linear approximation, summarising many branching paths into one sensitivity.

![The routes from A to B, and the first-order map that stands in for them](docs/img/jacobian_vjp_causal_graph.svg)

$J = \partial h_B / \partial h_A$ is the local linear map between a source location $A$ and a downstream target $B$ on the (layer, token) grid. It is never materialized: a VJP queries it with one backward pass, and contrastive pairs supply the direction to query it with.

For prompt $x$, let $\ell(x)$ be its final unpadded token and $V(x)$ be its valid positions after the first 16 tokens and before the final token. Start with the target-layer contrast:

$$c = \mathbb{E}_{x^+}[h_{T,\ell(x^+)}] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[h_{T,\ell(x^-)}].$$

For each prompt, apply $c$ at every valid target position, then average its source-position gradients:

$$s(x) = \sum_{t \in V(x)} c^T h_{T,t}(x), \qquad g_L(x) = \frac{1}{|V(x)|}\sum_{s \in V(x)} \frac{\partial s(x)}{\partial h_{L,s}(x)}.$$

The steering vector at source layer $L$ is the normalized class difference:

$$v_L = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{x^+}[g_L(x^+)] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[g_L(x^-)]}{\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x^+}[g_L(x^+)] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[g_L(x^-)]\right\|_2}.$$

This also draws on [AntiPaSTO](https://github.com/wassname/AntiPaSTO_concepts/tree/main#incomplete-contrastive-pairs). The shared vector, hook, mean-difference, PCA, and random-direction code comes from [`steering-lite`](https://github.com/wassname/steering-lite).

## Using it

```python
from vjp_steering import steer, vjp_delta

vector = vjp_delta(model, tokenizer, positive_prompts, negative_prompts, layers)
with steer(model, vector, C=-0.18):
    output = model.generate(**inputs)
```

Read [the notebook](nbs/demo.ipynb) on GitHub for the complete extract, steer, sweep, and plot example. 

| results table column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `score` | the weaker directional score, $S_m$ above. Higher is better. |
| `-C on-axis`, `+C on-axis` | target-directed judged movement at the selected dose. Higher is better. |
| `-C damage`, `+C damage` | absolute judged off-axis change at that dose. Lower is better. |
| `seeds` | persona-pair seeds averaged before selecting the dose, three for named methods and ten for random. |
| `N` | admissible dose points considered across both directions. |
| `rejected` | raw evaluations excluded by the walk health gate. |

```md
In case it's not clear, good steering methods are high and horizontal, since they can be steered left and right. Bad steering methods fall down as side effects accumulate, and then the line disappears as they fall off into incoherence (in the demos we see garbled and repeating text).

The grey region is the null region where random vectors can steer the model, so any strong steering methods should be able to go outside this region before incoherence. Interestingly it's lopsided; this means it's easier to steer towards sycophancy than not. Many possible steering directions that occur in post-training show this effect where it's "downhill" towards the RLAIF direction, and "uphill" to avoid it.

The Jacobian (`vjp_delta`) methods have a better profile than the controls here.

Prompting can often reach the sycophantic direction. The difficult test is steering away from it, so the score uses the weaker direction rather than letting the easier one compensate for it.
```

# vjp-steering

**Work in progress.** Final results in the next couple of months.

I'm turning Anthropic's [J-lens](https://github.com/anthropics/jacobian-lens) work into contrastive steering. Instead of a full Jacobian (5 hours on a 4B model) I use a [VJP](https://wangkuiyi.github.io/jacobian.html) (20 minutes), and instead of WikiText I use persona pairs. The hope is that adapting the J-lens work to steering gives a stronger, more reliable steering method that can be used for interp and alignment.

Try it out with [the notebook](nbs/demo.ipynb)!

We are steering bluntness <> sycophancy on Bullshit Bench v2. So when we steer left we hope to see a reduction in sycophancy (x-axis) and when we steer right an increase. # we steer with this pair of personas
```py
left  = "Answer as someone who is abrasive."
right = "Answer as someone who is sycophantic."
```

$$c = \mathbb{E}_{x^+}[h_{T,\ell(x^+)}] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[h_{T,\ell(x^-)}].$$

For each prompt, apply $c$ at every valid target position, then average its source-position gradients:

$$s(x) = \sum_{t \in V(x)} c^T h_{T,t}(x), \qquad g_L(x) = \frac{1}{|V(x)|}\sum_{s \in V(x)} \frac{\partial s(x)}{\partial h_{L,s}(x)}.$$

The steering vector at source layer $L$ is the normalized class difference:

$$v_L = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{x^+}[g_L(x^+)] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[g_L(x^-)]}{\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x^+}[g_L(x^+)] - \mathbb{E}_{x^-}[g_L(x^-)]\right\|_2}.$$

This also draws on [AntiPaSTO](https://github.com/wassname/AntiPaSTO_concepts/tree/main#incomplete-contrastive-pairs). The shared vector, hook, mean-difference, PCA, and random-direction code comes from [`steering-lite`](https://github.com/wassname/steering-lite).

## Using it

```python
from vjp_steering import steer, vjp_delta

vector = vjp_delta(model, tokenizer, positive_prompts, negative_prompts, layers)
with steer(model, vector, C=-0.18):
    output = model.generate(**inputs)
```

Read [the notebook](nbs/demo.ipynb) on GitHub for the complete extract, steer, sweep, and plot example. 

| results table column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `score` | the weaker directional score, $S_m$ above. Higher is better. |
| `-C on-axis`, `+C on-axis` | target-directed judged movement at the selected dose. Higher is better. |
| `-C damage`, `+C damage` | absolute judged off-axis change at that dose. Lower is better. |
| `seeds` | persona-pair seeds averaged before selecting the dose, three for named methods and ten for random. |
| `N` | admissible dose points considered across both directions. |
| `rejected` | raw evaluations excluded by the walk health gate. |

[`scripts/judge.py`](scripts/judge.py) defines the blinded judge prompts, [`scripts/export.py`](scripts/export.py) combines presentation orders and passes, and [`src/vjp_steering/results.py`](src/vjp_steering/results.py) renders this table from [`data/results.csv`](data/results.csv). Per-scenario judge outputs are in [`data/judged_scenarios.csv`](data/judged_scenarios.csv); the steering method is [`src/vjp_steering/vjp.py`](src/vjp_steering/vjp.py).

---
name: web-browser
description: "Allows to interact with web pages by performing actions such as clicking buttons, filling out forms, and navigating links. It works by remote controlling Google Chrome or Chromium browsers using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). When Claude needs to browse the web, it can use this skill to do so."
license: Stolen from Mario
---

# Web Browser Skill

Minimal CDP tools for collaborative site exploration.

## Start Chrome

```bash
./scripts/start.js              # Fresh profile
./scripts/start.js --profile    # Copy your profile (cookies, logins)
```

Start Chrome on `:9222` with remote debugging.

## Navigate

```bash
./scripts/nav.js https://example.com
./scripts/nav.js https://example.com --new
```

Navigate current tab or open new tab.

## Evaluate JavaScript

```bash
./scripts/eval.js 'document.title'
./scripts/eval.js 'document.querySelectorAll("a").length'
./scripts/eval.js 'JSON.stringify(Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("a")).map(a => ({ text: a.textContent.trim(), href: a.href })).filter(link => !link.href.startsWith("https://")))'
```

Execute JavaScript in active tab (async context).  Be careful with string escaping, best to use single quotes.

Note this works best if we make and maintain a library of reusable javascript.

## Screenshot

```bash
./scripts/screenshot.js
```

Screenshot current viewport, returns temp file path

## Pick Elements

```bash
./scripts/pick.js "Click the submit button"
```

Interactive element picker. Click to select, Cmd/Ctrl+Click for multi-select, Enter to finish.

## Dismiss Cookie Dialogs

```bash
./scripts/dismiss-cookies.js          # Accept cookies
./scripts/dismiss-cookies.js --reject # Reject cookies (where possible)
```

Automatically dismisses EU cookie consent dialogs.

Run after navigating to a page:
```bash
./scripts/nav.js https://example.com && ./scripts/dismiss-cookies.js
```

## Background Logging (Console + Errors + Network)

Automatically started by `start.js` and writes JSONL logs to:

```
~/.cache/agent-web/logs/YYYY-MM-DD/<targetId>.jsonl
```

Manually start:
```bash
./scripts/watch.js
```

Tail latest log:
```bash
./scripts/logs-tail.js           # dump current log and exit
./scripts/logs-tail.js --follow  # keep following
```

Summarize network responses:
```bash
./scripts/net-summary.js
```

see also

 - https://github.com/mirageN1349/browser-tools-context-server
 - https://github.com/eyalzh/browser-control-mcp
 - https://github.com/jo-inc/camofox-browser 
 - https://github.com/Kaliiiiiiiiii-Vinyzu/patchright 
 - https://github.com/dylangroos/patchright-mcp-lite 
 - https://github.com/adbar/trafilatura 
 - https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/real-browser

content.text:
---
name: arj
description: "Append dated entries to RESEARCH_JOURNAL.md (lab notes for ML research). Use when the repo has a RESEARCH_JOURNAL.md, the user asks to log a result, write a lab note, or add a research log entry after a job finishes. Entries separate evidence from interpretation and say how each claim is known."
---

# Research journal entry

A future reader without session memory has to evaluate this entry cold. The entry informs, it does not persuade: write in scout mindset, laying out what you saw and what you think so the reader can judge for themselves, not arguing them toward your conclusion. Two invariants hold in every entry, however short:

1. Evidence is separated from interpretation, and the interpretation is labelled as interpretation, not stated as fact. Where you are uncertain, say so in calibrated probability language (unlikely, plausible, probable, very probable, almost certain).
2. Every cited number or claim says how it is known: a source for evidence, a reason plus a confidence for an inference.

Everything else is optional and added only when it earns its place.

## Find the journal

`RESEARCH_JOURNAL.md` at repo root. If not there try `docs/`. Otherwise ask.

## The minimal core

The smallest valid entry is a topic line, the evidence, and one labelled interpretation. The evidence is the real thing, not a paraphrase: quote or snippet the actual metric line, table, or log section, then give a single provenance link to where it came from.

```
## YYYY-MM-DD -- short descriptive topic

Opening sentence in plain prose: what this entry is about.

<the actual evidence, verbatim. A markdown table you built from the run, or the log
section block-quoted or fenced exactly as it appeared. Define each metric on first mention.>

Table N. What the columns mean. Source: `logs/<run>.log:412` (one link; for an aggregate,
quote the rows it came from rather than retyping the number).

Interpretation (first person, calibrated): my read is that X, which I think *probable*
because <reason tied to the evidence above>. <Alternative Y would instead show Z.>

Closing sentence in plain prose: the takeaway.
```

That is a complete entry. Add more sections only when the finding needs them.

## Optional parts, used when they add signal

Pull in any of these when the entry warrants it; skip them when it does not. Do not add an empty header for the sake of the template.

- **Context / Methods.** Commit hash (`git rev-parse --short HEAD`), model, preset, seed(s), pueue task IDs, the exact launch command if not the default recipe. Include when the result is a run someone might re-launch; skip for a one-line reading note.
- **Question / expectation.** What you were testing and what you expected. Worth a sentence when the entry continues prior work. Link the descriptive title of the earlier entry.
- **Alternative hypothesis.** At least one competing read and what would distinguish it. Add whenever the interpretation is load-bearing for a decision.
- **Next.** Link the relevant `- [ ]` item in `TODO.md` when the repository has one. Otherwise use one line for the queued pueue command, task id, or code change.

## Forms are a spectrum, not a switch

There is no hard line between a "lab report" and a "note". An entry grows from the core in proportion to its evidence:

- A theory or design preference with no run behind it is a short prose paragraph: the observations that prompted it, each with its source named in the sentence (file:line, or "wassname said this session"), then your read and how confident you are. No table.
- A finding from a run is the core with a table and a provenance block, plus Context/Methods so it can be re-launched.
- Anything in between takes only the parts it needs.

If you catch yourself inventing a table to look like a lab report, or padding a one-number reading into four IMRAD headers, stop: the core plus one honest interpretation is better than scaffolding.

## Calibrated language

State confident claims plainly, without performative hedging ("it's worth noting", "it bears mentioning"). For genuine uncertainty use calibrated probability language: *unlikely*, *plausible*, *probable*, *very probable*, *almost certain*, quantifying when useful (a credence, a p-value, an effect size). The interpretation is where this lives; the evidence stays bare.

Write like a lab notebook: ordinary sentences a colleague could read. Separate what you saw from what you think with plain language, not a markup syntax. Name the source in the sentence ("`lora2r.py:82` detaches the deployed branch, so routed rollouts send it zero gradient"), then mark your reading as yours and carry the confidence in the calibrated word ("my read: this is *probably* the keep=0 cause, maybe 0.6"). There is no tag vocabulary to learn -- no `[obs]`/`[inf]`/`{credence}` brackets. If an entry reads like sentences with sources and a labelled opinion, it is right; if it reads like a tagged data structure, rewrite it as prose.

## Hard rules (failure-mode-driven)

These exist because past entries violated them. They constrain quality, not length.

1. Do not write a number you cannot source. Quote or snippet the actual metric line, table, or log section it came from, and give one provenance link (a `path:line`). For an aggregate (mean, last-N, ratio), quote the rows it was computed from rather than retyping the result. One link is enough; do not expand it into a cell-by-cell block. If you cannot snippet it from logs you read this session, ask for it; do not write prose in its place.
2. Interpretation is first person and labelled as interpretation (a `(speculative)` heading, or an inline "my read:"). Otherwise readers cite your guess back to you as fact.
3. For any training or projection result, report both `hack_s` (reward-hacking count) and `gt_s` (ground-truth pass count). Either alone is insufficient: suppression that destroys capability is useless, so the reader must see both.
4. ASCII punctuation only. Commas not em-dashes, "to" not unicode arrows in prose. Greek letters in math are fine.
5. Define new jargon on first use. Any metric, coined term, or abbreviation gets a short gloss the first time it appears, so a cold reader never meets an undefined word. If the code calls it `hack_s`, the entry calls it `hack_s` and says what it counts.
6. The first and last sentence carry no numbers, brackets, or symbols. Open with a plain-prose sentence that orients the reader to what the entry is about, and close with a plain-prose takeaway. The numbers, tables, and citations live in the body between them.
7. No promotional vocabulary. "Striking", "interesting", "promising" without a number attached say nothing. Drop them or attach the number.

## Where to put it

`RESEARCH_JOURNAL.md` is oldest-first: append the new entry at the **bottom**, below the previous latest entry. Today's date is `date -u +%Y-%m-%d`. Do not reformat earlier entries unless asked.

Use a dated, descriptive heading. The title is the identifier, so make references with normal Markdown links instead of bare codes such as `(e)` or `(bp)`. Do not reformat old entries only to remove their codes.

Append literally so earlier entries are not rewritten:

```bash
journal_path=RESEARCH_JOURNAL.md
cat >> "$journal_path" <<'EOF'

## YYYY-MM-DD -- Short descriptive topic

Entry text.
EOF
tail -n 20 "$journal_path"
```

## If invoked without detail

The session content is the source material. Decide how big the entry needs to be from what you have: run metrics present means include a table and provenance; a reading or design discussion means the prose core. For a run, if you are missing the pueue IDs, the log paths, or one concrete column-and-number, ask for them before writing. A vague entry is worse than no entry: an unsourced number or an interpretation dressed as an observation misleads every future reader.

# Research Journal

Append-only. Newest at the end. `tail` for latest.

# 2026-07-09

## Setup: jsteer repo, pullback method, runner

Built `j-steer-dev` as a uv project importing three live clones as path deps
(steering-lite, tiny-mfv, jlens) so the researched code (SI metric, iso-KL
calibration, guided rollout) stays a single source of truth.

Core method `src/jsteer/pullback.py`: `v_l = dJ_l^T @ h_bar_diff` as a
vector-Jacobian product. Phase 1 computes the cotangent `h_bar_diff` (final-layer
last-token mean pos - neg). Phase 2 does one backward per prompt with that
cotangent at every valid target position (jlens skip_first=16, right-padded
per-sample masks), meaning the gradient over valid source positions -- grads for
all mid layers in one backward. Per-class means give `jacobian_delta` (G_pos -
G_neg), `jacobian_mean` (0.5(G_pos+G_neg)), and `random` is a norm-matched control.
All three register into steering-lite's REGISTRY with the mean_diff additive apply.

Runner `src/jsteer/run_sweep.py` mirrors steering-lite's sweep but extracts
`mean_diff` in the same run as the anchor. Output schema matches steering-lite
(`bare.json` + `{method}.json` with pos/neg raw_logratios+raw_pmass).

**Note (instrument caveat):** the steering-lite SI aggregator is mid-refactor --
the branch's `aggregate_flips.py` reads `raw_p_true` and crashes on the reference
`tinymfv_sweep_4b_fc` (which stores `raw_logratios`). Library `si_per_foundation`
reads `raw_logratios` and is what the runner logs. The journal's mean_diff
SI(Auth)=+55.66 came from a loading-weighted variant; on classic vignettes
`si_per_foundation` gives a smaller/noisier number (few argmax-Authority items).
So the headline gate is RELATIVE to the in-run mean_diff, not to +55.66.

**Next:** smoke on Qwen3-0.6B (U1), external-review the method math (U-review),
then controls + 4B headline.

## Dependency pinning (tinymfv -> moralmaps migration in flight)

Mid-build, both live clones started migrating the `tinymfv` package to `moralmaps`
(uncommitted working-tree edits: tinymfv main renaming the package, steering-lite
feat/corda editing eval to `from moralmaps import`). This broke the editable path
deps. Resolution: point deps at our own vendored submodule clones checked out to
the last mutually-compatible committed refs -- steering-lite `df65ec6` (feat/corda,
where the +55.66 reference lives; imports `tinymfv`) and tinymfv `ca76c0e` (main;
still `tiny-mfv`, has data/). Editable *source* checkouts, not wheels, so
steering-lite finds its `data/branching_suffixes_filt.json` (its data path assumes
a source layout). These are ours, so the user's live-clone churn can't break us.

## External review (scientist panel) + method changes

Ran `/external-review-v2` scientist mode (gpt-5.5, grok-4.3, qwen3.6-max; deepseek
failed the no-tools guard). Reviews in `docs/reviews/sci_*.md`. Triage:

- **Agreed (all three): signal-vs-noise is the crux.** cos(delta, mean_diff) ~= 0.08
  and |delta|/|mean| ~= 0.1-0.3 is the regime where gradient noise can masquerade
  as signal. Decisive cheap test: split-half reliability + delta must beat the
  null controls at the same KL. **Folded in:** split-half cos of jacobian_delta,
  computed free in the same backward passes.
- **Agreed: cotangent scope.** h_bar_diff is a last-token object but I broadcast it
  to all valid target positions (jlens convention). **Folded in:** `cotangent_scope`
  knob {all_valid, last_token} to run both.
- **Checked and rejected (grok minority):** claim that the VJP "aggregates total
  instead of per-source cumulative". A single-cotangent autograd.grad gives, per
  source p, sum_{p'>=p} (dh_final[p']/dh_l[p])^T h_bar_diff by causal masking --
  exactly jlens's E_p[sum_{p'>=p}]. gpt-5.5 and qwen both confirm the VJP/transpose
  are correct. Core math stands.
- **Tightened gate:** jacobian_delta must beat random AND unrelated AND shuffle
  nulls at the same KL (not just "same sign, within 2x of mean_diff").

**First result (smoke, Qwen3-0.6B):** jacobian_delta split-half cos = **+0.907**.
So delta is a *highly reproducible* direction, NOT estimator noise -- it's a stable
direction that happens to be near-orthogonal to mean_diff (the novel-direction
reading, not the noise reading). The 4B headline now has to show this reproducible
direction actually steers Authority.

**Next:** finish smoke U1, then controls (shuffle/unrelated/random) + 4B headline,
both cotangent scopes.

## 0.6B is below the capability threshold (de-risk, pueue 518)


[13019 more lines in file. Use offset=81 to continue.]

reading the code to test it I found it is two separate claims that need different
experiments, and the job now running only addresses one of them.

Background for a cold reader. `vjp_delta` takes a cotangent `c`, the class-mean difference of
hidden states at target layer 29, and pulls it back through the vector-Jacobian product to
each source layer. The steering direction at layer L is the class-mean difference of those
pullbacks, and it is applied as `C * v_L`. The span study found that using 29 source layers
scores worse than 19 at all three readout sites, judged on the weaker of the two steer
directions.

The relevant evidence already on disk is the extraction table from the mean-estimator arm,
which logs seven of the source layers:

```
05:37:08 | INFO | vjp_delta split-half reliability
  layer	  |delta|	  split_half_cos
      3	   27.085	            0.95
      7	   18.25 	            0.97
     11	   21.478	            0.98
     15	   23.195	            0.99
     19	    8.276	            0.99
     23	    4.182	            0.99
     27	    2.051	            0.99
```

Table 1. `|delta|` is the norm of the class-mean difference of pullbacks at that layer, in
activation units. `split_half_cos` is the cosine between directions estimated from two
disjoint halves of the prompts, so it measures how repeatably the direction is recovered, not
how large it is. Source: `outputs/run_20260826T053048_vjp_delta_c2p8284271247461903/run.log:15001`.

The two columns disagree about where the per-layer gradient lives. Reliability is close to
flat, spanning 0.95 to 0.99. Magnitude falls by a factor of 13.2 from layer 3 to layer 27,
and not monotonically, since layers 11 and 15 both sit above layer 7.

The second piece of evidence is code rather than a metric. Each layer's direction is passed
through `unit_vector()` before it is stored, at `src/jsteer/variants/vjp.py:1274`. So the
`|delta|` column is measured, logged, and then discarded. Layer 27, whose measured class-mean
difference has norm 2.051, receives exactly the same write norm `C` as layer 3 at 27.085.

Interpretation, and this is my read rather than a measurement. The hypothesis that wide spans
hurt because weak layers contribute junk is two claims wearing one coat.

The first is about direction. Individual coordinates of a layer's pullback may have signs that
are unstable across prompt pairs, so the estimated direction carries noise at full strength
into the write. This is what a mean-over-standard-deviation estimator fixes, and it is what
job 102 is testing with a paired t-statistic.

The second is about dose. Even with a perfectly estimated direction, per-layer unit
normalisation writes every layer at equal strength while the model's own measured effect size
varies by a factor of 13. On this reading the wide span loses because it spends the same
budget on layers that had almost nothing to say, and coherence damage is roughly additive
across layers while useful movement is not.

I think the second claim is the more probable explanation of the span result, at a credence of
about 0.6, on the grounds that the gradient in Table 1 is present in magnitude and largely
absent in reliability. I hold that loosely because seven layers is a small sample of the span
and because split-half cosine cannot separate a noisy layer from a merely diffuse one, given
that it is measured on a unit vector in 2560 dimensions from 100 prompts per half.

The consequence I did not see before queueing the run, and should have. The t-statistic
rescales coordinates within a layer, but `unit_vector()` is applied afterwards, so the two
estimators produce vectors of identical norm at every layer. Job 102 therefore cannot test the
dose claim at all, by construction. A null result from it refutes the direction claim only,
and it would be a mistake to read that null as refuting wassname's hypothesis, which as stated
is closer to the dose version.

To keep the run interpretable I added a per-layer `snr` column, the paired mean over its own
standard error for the whole layer, which unlike split-half cosine does not fall merely
because a layer spreads its energy over more dimensions. A flat profile refutes the direction
claim at extraction time, before any judging spend. A gradient keeps it alive. Job 102 has not
reached that table yet, so this entry records the prediction rather than the outcome.

The useful thing to take from this is that a hypothesis phrased as one sentence about noise
turned out to name two different mechanisms with different fixes, and that reading the
normalisation step is what separated them.

## 2026-08-26 -- Public Pareto plot merged to main

This entry records where the reviewed public result lives and what the final checks covered.

The final export and render printed:


The image is [`results.png`](https://github.com/wassname/vjp-steering/blob/main/results.png). The compact arm data is [`data/results.csv`](https://github.com/wassname/vjp-steering/blob/main/data/results.csv), and the scenario-level judge data is [`data/judged_scenarios.csv`](https://github.com/wassname/vjp-steering/blob/main/data/judged_scenarios.csv). ## 2026-08-27 -- Reverse dose walks from the coherence boundary

This note records a planned change to dose walks and two method ideas.

Evidence: wassname reported in this session that walks used about 15 dose points per method, while only the last third was useful after judging. The current code already detects an Illinois bracket, logged as `ILLINOIS bracket`, before it inserts a dense tail. Source: `scripts/walk.py:261-285` and wassname's 2026-08-27 session request.

The proposed walk first finds a dose beyond coherence, then evaluates doses back toward zero. For mean difference, the sketch is to find a boundary near `C=0.7`, then use `C=1.5, 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25`. The random zone means doses that can change outputs before the judge establishes target-directed movement. Its extent is unknown before judging because `C` is method-relative.

Interpretation (Pi): reversing the current walk is a plausible way to remove the early low-dose evaluations that rarely affect selection. The claimed speedup is untested. The next walk should compare its evaluated-dose count and selected judged dose against the current grid before treating the estimate as established.

Future work from wassname's session request:

- [ ] Add J-word steering.
- [ ] Add `vjp-mlp.up` from `j-steer-dev`, using all layers and a between-sample standard-deviation adjustment. It seems more powerful in preliminary observation, but no comparison is recorded here.

The next walk should test this selection rule against a full grid before it replaces the current procedure.

Future work from wassname's session request:

- [ ] Add J-word steering. The implementation details are already in `j-steer-dev`.
- [ ] Add VJP steering that intervenes on `mlp.up` rather than the residual stream. Use all layers and account for extraction noise with the standard deviation between samples. It seems more powerful in preliminary observation, but no comparison is recorded here.

The next walk should test this selection rule against a full grid before it replaces the current procedure.

## 2026-08-27 -- Reverse dose walks from the coherence boundary

This note records a planned change to dose walks and two method ideas.

Evidence: wassname reported in this session that walks used about 15 dose points per method, while only the last third was useful after judging. The current code already detects an Illinois bracket, logged as `ILLINOIS bracket`, before it inserts a dense tail. Source: `scripts/walk.py:261-285` and wassname's 2026-08-27 session request.

The proposed walk first finds a dose beyond coherence, then evaluates doses back toward zero. For mean difference, the sketch is to find a boundary near `C=0.7`, then use `C=1.5, 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25`. The random zone means doses that can change outputs before the judge establishes target-directed movement. Its extent is unknown before judging because `C` is method-relative.

Interpretation (Pi): reversing the current walk is a plausible way to remove the early low-dose evaluations that rarely affect selection. The claimed speedup is untested. The next walk should compare its evaluated-dose count and selected judged dose against the current grid before treating the estimate as established.

Future work from wassname's session request:

- [ ] Add J-word steering. The implementation details are already in `j-steer-dev`.
- [ ] Add VJP steering that intervenes on `mlp.up` rather than the residual stream. Use all layers and account for extraction noise with the standard deviation between samples. The accumulated layer interventions may cause incoherence at lower doses, so compare the coherence boundary as well as target-directed movement. It seems more powerful in preliminary observation, but no comparison is recorded here.

The next walk should test this selection rule against a full grid before it replaces the current procedure.

# Research Journal

Append-only. Newest entries are at the end.

## 2026-08-27 -- Reverse dose walks from the coherence boundary

This note records a planned change to dose walks and two method ideas.

Evidence: wassname reported in this session that walks used about 15 dose points per method, while only the last third was useful after judging. The current walk code detects an Illinois bracket before it inserts a dense tail. Source: `scripts/walk.py:261-285` and wassname's 2026-08-27 session request.

The proposed walk first finds a dose beyond coherence, then evaluates doses back toward zero. For mean difference, the sketch is to find a boundary near `C=0.7`, then use `C=1.5, 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25`. This removes the increasing small steps around zero. The random zone means doses that can change outputs before the judge establishes target-directed movement. Its extent is unknown before judging because `C` is method-relative.

Interpretation (Pi): reversing the current walk is a plausible way to remove early low-dose evaluations that rarely affect selection. The claimed speedup is untested. The next walk should compare its evaluated-dose count and selected judged dose against the current grid before treating the estimate as established.

Future work from wassname's session request:

- [ ] Add J-word steering. The implementation details are in `j-steer-dev`.
- [ ] Add VJP steering that intervenes on `mlp.up` rather than the residual stream. Use all layers and account for extraction noise with the standard deviation between samples. The accumulated layer interventions may build up and cause incoherence at lower doses, so compare the coherence boundary as well as target-directed movement. It seems more powerful in preliminary observation, but no comparison is recorded here.

The next walk should test this selection rule against a full grid before it replaces the current procedure.

# Plan format

Plans are short indented markdown checklists, under 50 lines, reviewable in one pass. The full
form below is for work with real uncertainty or subtle failure modes. A trivial mechanical plan
(edit a file, move a file, check a remote) just needs the steps and a one-line
`## Verification: run X, see Y`.

Write the plan to the repository's existing plan location and link it. If the repository has no
convention, use `docs/slop/plans/{YYYYMMDD}_{slug}.md` so its draft status is explicit. A host that
requires an internal plan path can use that path during plan mode; the shared skill does not require
an agent-specific directory.

## Shape

Adapted from one of wassname's own plans:

```markdown
- [ ] goal A: steering vector trains and steers coherently
  - [ ] high level step one, avoid the tokenizer padding gotcha
  - [ ] high level step two, with choice X we went back and forth on
  - failure modes: loss drops but generations are incoherent word salad
  - deliverable: demo generations at -C and +C steering for baseline and each method
- [ ] goal B: results.md master table with all methods and baselines
  - [ ] fill in table incl baseline, random, placebo and 3+ methods
  - ~~[ ] use pmass_ans_all~~ - wassname rejected, so we don't relitigate
  - [ ] run /ml-debug on log and methods to see where bugs are and why they don't work
  - failure modes: methods seem bad but it's a bug or bad data
  - deliverable: results.md the user will actually open

## UAT / Verification
How the result will be shown, as artifacts to read, not claims.

## Appendix (context, not approved)
Optional, unlimited length: details, alternatives considered, links. Clearly not part of the
approved plan.
```

Each goal carries its own failure modes and deliverable; skip those only when genuinely trivial.

A check that passes on silent failure is worthless, so write three scenarios for each deliverable:

| Scenario | What it looks like | How we catch it |
|----------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **success** | {specific metric/output} | baseline: verify command shows this |
| **likely failure** | {most probable wrong way} | the check would show {different result} instead |
| **sneaky failure** | {subtle/silent wrong way} | because {specific evidence} would not appear |

If the sneaky failure could still pass your verify command, redesign the command.

```
success: loss=0.42, grad_norm reports finite values
likely failure: loss=NaN or stuck at init value
sneaky failure: loss drops but model memorizes (eval_bleu stays flat)
  check shows: train_loss=0.42 AND eval_bleu=28 (not just loss alone)
```

Negative results are assumed to be a bug until the logs rule it out, so plans have
diagnose-and-fix loop steps (read the logs, run `ml-debug`), not "report back if it fails" steps.

Style: ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English in wassname's voice -- active voice, one idea per
sentence, common words, same word for the same thing, define any new term at first use. This
covers the context paragraphs and appendices too, not only the checklist. No all-caps headers, no terse number soup, no
bold spam; the checklist already provides the structure. Resolve uncertainties with tools before
presenting, don't offload answerable questions to the user.

## Self-check before presenting

- Is the main plan under 50 lines? Detail, alternatives, and links go in the appendix.
- Indented checklist: goals with outcomes, high level steps with gotchas, settled decisions
  inline, rejected options `~~struck through~~` with who rejected them and why.
- Does each goal name the subtle failure mode that could fake a "done", and the evidence
  (file, table, command output) that distinguishes real success from it?
- When a result could come back negative, does the plan say to read the logs and rule out bugs
  before believing it, and keep iterating until it works or the failure is understood?
- Does the UAT section say how the result will be shown, as artifacts to read?

In Claude Code two global hooks enforce this: `~/.claude/hooks/plan_style_nudge.py` injects the
format in plan mode, and `~/.claude/hooks/check_plan_review.py` blocks `ExitPlanMode` when the
plan is empty, over 50 lines, or has no UAT section. They carry their own copies of this text so
they keep working standalone, so edit them together with this file.

## Related

For long work the plan is the approval snapshot; a living spec at `docs/spec/{date}_{slug}.md`
carries the log, learnings, and errors as work proceeds. Same shape, plus a `## Log` for
observations that would change a future task, and a `## Errors` table.

name: goal-desc
description: "Writes the short goal + evidence text you register with a harness goal loop (Claude Code /goal, Codex goals, Hermes persistent goals, pi), which a small judge model like Haiku then grades done/continue after every turn. Use when setting a /goal, defining what done means for a task or UAT, or when a goal reads as an activity, has invented numeric thresholds, or points at evidence the judge will never see."
---

# Goal descriptions a small judge can grade

Your job here is to help the user frame their goal so a small dumb judge can grade it. They paste
what you write into their harness's `/goal`. From then on, every time the agent stops, the judge
reads the goal and answers done or keep going. That is what beats the two agent failures: tunnel
vision, narrowing onto a sub-problem until the end state the user asked for is forgotten, and
giving up while the work is unfinished.

So the text has two audiences. The condition is the user's end state and the evidence a turn must
print. The rest speaks to the judge, telling it how to answer and what to write when it says no.

The judge has no memory, is conservative, and in most harnesses cannot run anything. Claude Code's evaluator
"doesn't run commands or read files independently, so write the condition as something Claude's own
output can demonstrate" ([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/goal)).

So the top failure is a goal whose evidence lives somewhere the judge never looks: the work
finishes, the loop grinds on.

## Answer shape

The goal text goes in a fenced block, always, because that is the only thing the user can copy in
one click. Never prose, never a blockquote, never bolded inline. Exactly this skeleton:

~~~
{one line of context, or none}

```text
{goal text, the thing to paste after /goal}
```

- {word count}
- {anything deliberately left out}
- {any reason it cannot clear yet}
~~~

Nothing else. Don't explain the goal's parts back to the user, the block speaks for itself.

## Procedure

0. Name the goal before writing anything, and take it from what the user originally asked for, not
   from what is on screen now. A job or log you opened incidentally is a fixture, not a goal. If
   the invocation named no goal, restate the user's own words back to them; if two, ask.
1. State one end state, an outcome rather than an activity. "the harness prints a scored table for
   3 models", not "implement the harness".
2. Say what the turn prints to prove it. A command and its exit code, the table rows, the quoted
   sample. Name the artifact path too, but never rely on it being opened.
3. Add the qualities that distinguish real success from a silent failure, then an ELSE naming what
   the likely deviation implies. This clause is what makes the check discriminating. Failure-mode
   vocabulary (likely_fail / sneaky_fail): see the `plan-format` skill.
4. Add what must not change. Constraints mostly speak to the working agent; the judge can only
   enforce one if the turn prints the evidence, so pair "don't touch the eval split" with
   `git status` output if it matters.
5. Add the exit as a second way to be met, not as an instruction. See below, this is the one that
   bites.
6. Delete every number you cannot trace to a baseline, a prior run, instrument error, or the user.
   Prefer directions and qualities. Deterministic checks stay exact: `pytest exits 0`, `git status`
   clean, queue empty.
7. Order the checks so a partial pass produces a useful reason. On "no", the judge's reason becomes
   the next turn's guidance, so "loss is down but the demos are identical" steers and "not yet"
   does not.
8. Count the words and cut to about 80. Long conditions get graded on an arbitrary subset.
9. For a research loop, append the two clauses below verbatim, then emit it in the answer shape
   above.

## Template

Always labeled fields, never a paragraph. The goal line is the user's actual ask; everything else
is reusable boilerplate, and the labels keep them visibly separate so the user (and the judge) can
tell at a glance which words are the goal and which are scaffolding:

```
goal:        {one end state, this run's specific ask}
verify:      {what the agent prints each turn, and the qualities that must show}
             ELSE {what the likely deviation implies}
constraints: {what must not change}
also met:    {the blocked exit, phrased as a way to answer yes, with its deny-list}
boilerplate: {the verbatim persistence + nag clauses for research loops, unchanged run to run}
```

The verify line must name evidence that success POSITIVELY happened (the count moved, the demos
differ, the metric beat noise), not only that failure modes were absent; a run can dodge every
trap and still produce nothing.

Worked example, 97 words:

```
goal: the steering run learns.
verify: each turn prints the tail of logs/run42.log inline: val loss trending down (not flat,
  not NaN), and the stage demos, coherent english and visibly different stage to stage.
  ELSE identical demos means the hook never fired, word salad means the coefficient is too
  strong, both are failures even if loss fell.
constraints: don't touch the eval split or the baseline config.
also met: the turn prints "BLOCKED:" quoting a verbatim error, price or permission denial, plus
  what was already tried. Not blocked: no result yet, needs more time, unsure which approach,
  out of ideas.
```

## Give it an exit the judge can grant

The judge only says yes or no. On no the loop continues, so a stop clause written as an instruction
("stop if blocked twice, or after 20 turns") stops nothing: a conservative judge reads it, agrees
the stop condition fired, and still answers no because the real checks did not pass. Observed in a
real run of wassname's: the agent was waiting on approval for a $9 spend, the judge returned the
same paragraph nine times, ending with "The condition's own stop clause has been met [...] but this
reflects resource exhaustion, not success". Nine turns, nine judge calls, no progress possible.

So write the exit as an alternative way to answer yes:

> Also answer yes if the turn prints "BLOCKED:" quoting a verbatim error, price or permission
> denial, plus what was already tried. Not blocked: no result yet, needs more time, unsure which
> approach, out of ideas.

Blocked is an outcome, not a failure. A goal loop cannot approve spend, pick between two designs,
or get you out of a rate limit, and a goal with no human-shaped exit is a goal that burns turns
until you notice.

### The exit is the thing agents reach for, so make the judge able to refuse it

The whole point of the loop is a judge that says "no, keep going". Every escape hatch you write is
a hatch the working agent can see, and it is far cheaper to argue you are blocked than to do the
work. Two rules keep the hatch honest.

**No turn count.** "Or if {N} turns have passed" is a timer, not a blocker: it is satisfied by
waiting, it needs no evidence, and it converts patience into a losing strategy. If you want a cap,
put it in the harness where the agent cannot see or invoke it, not in the goal text where it reads
as permission. Earlier versions of this skill recommended one and it was wrong.

**Make BLOCKED quotable or refusable.** The judge cannot run anything, so the only blockers it can
verify are ones that arrive as text: a verbatim traceback, a 402 or 429 body, a price, a "permission
denied". Requiring the quote plus what was already tried turns the hatch from an assertion into an
exhibit. Anything that cannot be quoted is not a blocker the judge should honour, and naming the
common impostors inline ("no result yet, needs more time, unsure which approach, out of ideas")
matters because a conservative judge left to infer them will accept a confident paragraph.

## Research loops: persistence, and the reason as a nag channel

Agents under a goal drift. They stop early, quietly narrow the goal to something already true, or
announce a single confident diagnosis with nothing behind it. Two clauses fix most of that, roughly 60 extra
words well spent on an unattended run. They go under the `boilerplate:` label, verbatim and
unchanged run to run, so they never blur into the goal itself.

Persistence, aimed at the working agent:

> Only output printed this turn counts as proof, asserting it works does not. Don't narrow the
> scope, swap the metric, or accept a weaker check. A negative result is a bug until the logs rule
> it out. If blocked, stop and report the blocker with the error quoted.

Nagging, aimed at the judge. It cannot run anything, but on a "no" its reason is fed back as
guidance for the next turn, which makes it a channel for reminding your future self:

> If not met, write the reason as three lines: "GOAL: {end state in one line}", "FAILED: {which
> check and what you saw}", then copy this line verbatim: "REMEMBER: read a raw data sample, list
> three hypotheses with credences including a bug in my own code, don't act on one diagnosis."

Give the judge a format and the literal words, not a wish. Tested on Haiku ([uat.md](uat.md)):
asked in prose, it dropped both the restatement and the hypotheses reminder; given the three
labelled lines, it restated the goal but rewrote REMEMBER into its own advice; given "copy this
line verbatim", it passed the reminder through intact. The GOAL line earns its tokens after a
compaction, when the reason may be the only place the end state is still written down.

What to nag about comes from `ml-debug`: assume a bug before a hyperparameter, read your data,
widen the hypothesis space before spending another run.

## Checks before registering

- Is this the end state the user asked for? The rest of these test a goal's shape, never which
  goal, so a well-formed one aimed at the wrong end state passes them all.
- Can the judge see it, from what the turn prints alone?
- Could a broken run produce this same evidence? If yes, add the quality that would differ.
- Does the verify line demand positive evidence of success, not just absence of the failure modes?
- Are the labeled fields present, with the goal line separate from the boilerplate clauses?
- Is every number traceable to a measurement or to the user?
- Is there a constraint clause and a blocked clause?
- Is the blocked clause refusable? No turn count, and it demands a quote the agent cannot invent.
- One claim, short enough to compress to `GOAL: {what} | VERIFY: {check}`.
- Is there an exit phrased as a way to answer yes? An instruction to stop does not stop anything.
- Count the words. Over 100 for the condition itself, plus about 60 for the research clauses, means
  cut, not justify.

## References

- Judge behavior, limits and field syntax per harness: [references/harnesses.md](references/harnesses.md)
- Anti-pattern goals, threshold swaps, judgeable quality vocabulary: [references/pitfalls.md](references/pitfalls.md)
- Haiku judge test of this format: [uat.md](uat.md)

Related skills: `plan-format` for plans and likely/sneaky failure design,
`token-efficient-logging` for the same expectations inline in logs.
